title: Standing, sitting, lying down
hookLine: those who remember Allah in every posture and reflect on creation: You did not make this in vain (3:190–191)

lines: THE PROPHET LOOKS AT THE SKY.
cards: A boy named Ibn Abbas, the Prophet's young cousin, once spent the night at the house of his aunt Maymunah, one of the Prophet's wives. He had come, the reports say, to see how the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night.

In the last part of the night, he saw him get up, look at the sky, and begin to recite. Bukhari records what he recited: the last verses of Al 'Imran. Today the surah ends with them, under the same sky.

teach.b: Verse 190 says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding.
Verse 191 says who they are: those who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth.
And what they say, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." Then: glory be to You, protect us from the punishment of the Fire.
Three postures cover almost every moment of a human life: work, rest, sleep, sickness. Remembrance isn't tied to one position or one hour. The same three show up in a hadith about prayer.
A sick companion asked how to pray, and the Prophet told him: standing; if you can't, then sitting; if you can't, then on your side. Nobody is too weak to be counted.
Then the second act: reflection, tafakkur. Not just looking at the stars, but thinking until a conclusion comes out of your mouth: You didn't make this in vain.
Batil, the word for in vain, means empty, pointless, false. The people in the verse look at the night sky and conclude the opposite.

teach.h: THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.
teach.b: So the surah that began with clear and ambiguous verses ends here, after the chosen family, Maryam, the rope, Uhud and its grief, and death tasted: a person under the night sky, in whatever posture they can manage, saying: not in vain.

how: Some Muslims recite the last verses of Al 'Imran (3:190–200) when they wake for the night prayer, following the Prophet's practice reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, and remember God in whatever posture they're in throughout the day.

o: remembering God in every posture, at any hour
rising from sleep to pray before dawn each day
keeping one fixed position through the whole prayer

games.q: the last verses of Al 'Imran — tap the pairs.
p: watched the Prophet recite at night

s: remembrance in 3:191 needs a special posture
standing, sitting, or lying down: every posture counts.
the Prophet recited these verses when he woke at night
Bukhari reports Ibn Abbas saw him look at the sky and recite them.
the verse asks only for looking at creation
it asks for reflection, tafakkur, that ends in words: not in vain.

games.q: you're sick and can't stand for the prayer. according to the hadith, what do you do?
o: skip the prayer until you're well.
pray sitting; if you can't, then on your side.
ask someone else to pray for you.
games.why: standing; if not, sitting; if not, on your side. the same three postures as 3:191.

practice: Choose your posture, stand, sit or lie down, whichever your body wants, and picture the night sky: the dark, the scattered lights, the distances.

Let the size of it settle on you until one thought forms slowly, the way it did for the people in the verse: this is not pointless. If you pray, you can say the verse's own words: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.

wordCard.voice: Standing. Standing, sitting, and lying down: remembering God in every posture, and reflecting on creation, from 3:191. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: standing, and sitting, and on their sides (3:191).

carryVoice: Your line: not in vain. Any posture will do. That's Al 'Imran, start to finish.
